clue.text: Masculine queen's presented with something like gorse in this Highlands story

parts.note: butch means masculine in manner or looks
ER (Elizabeth Regina) is the usual crossword queen, with the possessive 's kept
broom is a yellow-flowered shrub of the same family as gorse

explanation.surface: A manly queen is handed a gorse-like shrub in a Scottish Highland tale.
explanation.walkthrough: Neil Gunn's novel of the Highland Clearances shares its name with a prickly evergreen shrub; 'presented with' simply joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Neil Gunn's 1934 novel set in the Scottish Highlands bears this title.

clue.text: Wilder character — one writing about bridge problem

definitions.meaning: a friar in Thornton Wilder's The Bridge of San Luis Rey
the friar investigates and writes a book about the collapse of the bridge

explanation.surface: A character of Wilder's who writes on bridge puzzles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bridge problem' suggests the card game, but the problem is a rope bridge in Peru falling with five people on it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Franciscan friar in Thornton Wilder's novel records the lives of those killed when the bridge collapses.

clue.text: Atlas, who was in Jason's crew

definitions.meaning: an atlas is a carved male figure used as a column supporting a building
one of the Argonauts, father of Ajax

explanation.surface: Atlas, as one of the Argonauts.
explanation.walkthrough: Atlas the Titan was no Argonaut; here 'Atlas' is the architectural figure.
explanation.definitionFit: A sculpted male column is an atlas or its synonym; and the Greek hero, father of Ajax, sailed with Jason.

clue.text: Queen and duchess, chosen by director to be embraced by drag character in a famous comedy

indicators.note: the inner pieces are held inside the word for drag

parts.note: to hale is to drag or haul
R (Regina) stands for queen
D is an abbreviation for duchess
actors chosen by a director are cast

explanation.surface: Royal and aristocratic ladies, picked by a director, are hugged by a cross-dressing figure in a classic comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drag' suggests cross-dressing but is HALE, which holds R, D and CAST.
explanation.definitionFit: Squire Hardcastle and his family are central figures in Goldsmith's comedy She Stoops to Conquer.

clue.text: Pound sign

definitions.meaning: to pound is to strike forcefully, to batter
Aries, the zodiac sign, is symbolised by a male sheep

explanation.surface: A symbol for a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound sign' suggests £; the words split into two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: To batter is to pound something hard, and Aries is the zodiac sign of the male sheep.

clue.text: In medieval verse, you may see this personage returning to duke with a traitor

definitions.text: In medieval verse, you may see this

indicators.note: returning means coming back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a nabob is a wealthy person of importance
a heel is a treacherous, contemptible person

explanation.surface: In a medieval poem, an important figure goes back to a duke alongside a traitor.
explanation.walkthrough: The stanza form of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight ends with a short line followed by a rhyming quatrain; 'returning' turns NABOB into BOBAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Medieval alliterative poetry such as Sir Gawain ends its stanzas with this short-line pattern.

clue.text: Working the good earth, an agricultural slave in Poland

definitions.text: Working the good earth, an agricultural slave

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the name of the country

explanation.surface: A slave toiling on the land in Poland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the good earth' points to Pearl Buck's novel The Good Earth.
explanation.definitionFit: In Pearl Buck's The Good Earth, Wang Lung's wife was a kitchen slave before working the fields beside him.

clue.text: A sailor and his fate — remaining a sailor

parts.note: a mate is a ship's officer, a sailor
one's lot is one's fate

explanation.surface: A seaman and his destiny: to stay at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'remaining' is a link: the wordplay remains as the defined word.
explanation.definitionFit: Matelot is British slang, from French, for a seaman.

clue.text: Character in parliamentary stories, punished for seeing Prime Minister

definitions.meaning: a son of the Duke of Omnium in Trollope's Palliser novels, which centre on politics
he is sent down from Cambridge for going to the Derby, where his brother's horse Prime Minister ran

explanation.surface: A figure in political novels disciplined for visiting the head of government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prime Minister' looks like the man in Downing Street (or his father, who was PM), but it is the racehorse.
explanation.definitionFit: In Trollope's The Duke's Children, the Duke's younger son is rusticated after slipping off to the Derby.

clue.text: Container for fuel I found in decrepit Scottish island

indicators.note: the letter is said to be found within the word for decrepit, so it goes inside

parts.note: decrepit means old and worn out
Rum is an island of the Inner Hebrides off western Scotland

explanation.surface: Someone finds a fuel container on a run-down Scottish island.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrel of the kind used to store and ship petroleum is exactly a fuel container.

clue.text: Carry king into conflict, as a character in a story involving a feud

definitions.text: as a character in a story involving a feud

indicators.note: the king's letter is put into the word for conflict

parts.note: a battle is an armed conflict
R (Rex) is the standard abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: An instruction to bear a monarch into the fray, like someone in a tale of feuding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carry' looks like a verb but is the first name: Carry Brattle is the fallen woman in Trollope's The Vicar of Bullhampton, whose plot turns on the vicar's feud with the Marquis of Trowbridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Carry Brattle is a figure in Trollope's novel The Vicar of Bullhampton, built round a quarrel between vicar and marquis.

clue.text: Pinter's work in gnomic production

parts.note: to be in is to be at home

indicators.note: a production of the letters makes something new from them, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Harold Pinter play staged in an enigmatic, cryptic manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a link word but gives HOME; 'production' rearranges GNOMIC into COMING.
explanation.definitionFit: Harold Pinter's 1965 play is titled The Homecoming.

clue.text: Opponent of slavery — his poems stir trouble up

indicators.note: to stir is to mix, so the letters are churned
in a down clue, up means the word reads upwards, from bottom to top

parts.note: to ail is to trouble

explanation.surface: An abolitionist whose verses cause unrest.
explanation.walkthrough: St Clare's Vermont cousin in Uncle Tom's Cabin opposes slavery in principle.
explanation.definitionFit: In Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel, St Clare's cousin from Vermont is an abolitionist in her views.

clue.text: Durrell's work that's mostly an easy read

indicators.note: mostly means most of the word is kept, its last letter dropped

parts.note: text that is clear is an easy read

explanation.surface: A Lawrence Durrell novel that is, on the whole, light going.
explanation.definitionFit: The final volume of Lawrence Durrell's Alexandria Quartet has this title.

clue.text: He wrote about schoolboys — a young man brought up, for example, in a bad way

parts.note: a buck is a dashing young man

indicators.note: in a down clue, brought up means the letters climb, read upwards

parts.note: EG is the abbreviation of exempli gratia, for example
dire means in a bad way, dreadful

explanation.surface: An author of school stories: a lad poorly raised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought up' reverses the two pieces after 'a young man' as one run; 'young man' tempts as the schoolboy subject, but it is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Buckeridge wrote the Jennings stories about a boys' prep school.

clue.text: Old English characters, and rare French ones?

parts.note: in French the feminine plural of 'one' is unes

explanation.surface: Ancient English letters, and some uncommon French ones too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rare' is not describing the French characters: it gives R, and 'French ones' gives UNES.
explanation.definitionFit: The letters of the Anglo-Saxon futhorc alphabet were carved symbols of this kind.

clue.text: Spotted, cleaned, or covered in waste particles

parts.note: spotted means saw or noticed
dusted means cleaned of dust

explanation.surface: A list of things done to a floor: spotted, cleaned, or strewn with debris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' reads as marked with spots, but means noticed.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprinkled with the fine shavings a saw leaves behind, as a workshop floor is.

clue.text: A Coleridge poem, rather like The Ancient Mariner

definitions.meaning: a poem by Mary Elizabeth Coleridge, the great-grandniece of Samuel Taylor Coleridge, carries this title
the Mariner detains the wedding guest against his will, an intruder nobody asked for

explanation.surface: A Coleridge poem, compared with his most famous ballad.
explanation.walkthrough: The obvious Coleridge is Samuel Taylor, author of The Ancient Mariner, but the poem is by Mary Coleridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Mary Coleridge wrote the poem; and the Mariner, buttonholing a guest bound for a wedding, is a guest no one wanted.

clue.text: One making a forest home, to win the affection of a poet, mostly

parts.note: to woo is to court

indicators.note: mostly means the poet's name loses its last letter

parts.note: Dante is the Italian poet

explanation.surface: Someone settling in the woods while courting a poet.
explanation.definitionFit: This insect builds large mound nests in woodland.

clue.text: Rope reportedly presented by a famous director

indicators.note: reportedly says the word is heard rather than seen, so its sound is what counts

parts.note: a cord is a thin rope

explanation.surface: A celebrated film-maker offers up a rope, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: Alexander Korda was a Hungarian-British film producer and director; Rope is also a Hitchcock film, a neat distraction.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander Korda made The Private Life of Henry VIII and produced The Third Man, a renowned film-maker.

clue.text: Poet's whisky pined for in broadcast

indicators.note: broadcast means said on air, so the sound is what matters

parts.note: rye is a whisky; pined for means missed

explanation.surface: A poet longs for whisky on air.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhymist is a writer of verse, a versifier.

clue.text: One-trick wonder, as a person

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
a con is a trick or swindle

explanation.surface: A one-hit wonder as a celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One-trick' reads as one adjective, but splits into One (I) and trick (CON).
explanation.definitionFit: A person revered as a wonder or idol is a celebrated figure of this kind.

clue.text: Juvenile stag of a special kind in a tale of Scottish history

parts.note: a juvenile is a child
a royal is a stag with twelve or more points to its antlers

explanation.surface: A young deer of a particular type appears in a story of Scotland's past.
explanation.definitionFit: A historical novel set in Scotland carries this title.

clue.text: Philosopher Henry introducing you to me

parts.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
U stands for you in text speak

explanation.surface: A philosopher called Henry makes introductions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Henry' looks like a first name for the philosopher; it is the unit H.
explanation.definitionFit: David Hume was the Scottish Enlightenment philosopher.

clue.text: Swedenborg's rejected European currency denomination

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the whole run is read in reverse

parts.note: the leu is the currency of Romania and Moldova
a denomination is a name

explanation.surface: The Swedish mystic's turned-down coinage of a European note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns LEU and NAME together into EMANUEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Emanuel was the given name of the Swedish mystic and scientist Swedenborg.

clue.text: Installs roads in complex

indicators.note: complex as an adjective means tangled, so the letters are knotted into a new order

explanation.surface: A planner puts roads into a road complex.
explanation.definitionFit: To ordain someone is to install them formally in priestly office.

clue.text: "With thunders from her native - / She quells the floods below" (Thomas Campbell)

definitions.text: "With thunders from her native - / She quells the floods below" (Thomas Campbell)

parts.words: "With thunders from her native - / She quells the floods below" (Thomas Campbell)
parts.note: fill the gap in Campbell's Ye Mariners of England with the tree whose timber built Britain's warships

explanation.surface: A line from Campbell's naval poem with a word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: British men-of-war were built of this hardwood, so Britannia thunders from her native timber.

clue.text: A story of Harris — comic character following dog's lead into a boat

indicators.note: the comic character comes after the boat piece
the dog's lead is put into the boat

parts.note: the Ark is Noah's famous boat

indicators.note: a dog's lead taken as its leading letter

parts.note: a jester is a court clown

explanation.surface: A Harris tale in which a clown follows a dog on its lead into a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilson Harris, the Guyanese novelist, wrote The Dark Jester (2001); 'lead' gives the first letter of dog, D, which goes into THE ARK.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilson Harris's 2001 novel about Pizarro and Atahualpa is The Dark Jester.
